_meta.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (AH-66), The Commercial Storage of Fruits, Vegetables, and Florist and Nursery Stocks
_meta.generated_for: Smart Shelf — ESP32 spoilage-monitoring shelf, MSME kirana stores
_meta.note: Respiration rates are mg CO2 kg-1 h-1. Q10 is computed per commodity from the two closest data points to typical kirana ambient range and is NOT constant across temperature — Handbook 66 data tops out at 20-25 C, while Indian kirana ambient can exceed that (30-40 C). Using these Q10 values above 25 C is an extrapolation beyond measured data — flag this explicitly in any report/defense.

units.respiration: mg CO2 per kg per hour

tomato.chilling_note: Mature-green fruit below 13 C risks chilling injury (pitting, uneven ripening). Ripe tomato tolerates down to 10 C without visible CI but loses flavor/aroma.
tomato.ethylene_note: Moderate producer, highly sensitive to external ethylene — as little as 0.5 uL/L triggers ripening.

onion.variant_assumed: dry/pungent (cured) — most relevant for kirana shelf stock, not green/bunching onions
onion.chilling_note: Not chilling sensitive. Freezes at -0.8 C; injury risk below -4 C. Sprouting accelerates above 4 C ambient — the practical concern for a kirana shelf is sprouting/rot from heat and humidity, not chilling.
onion.ethylene_note: Very low producer, low sensitivity. Only very high ethylene (>1500 uL/L) encourages sprouting.

potato.chilling_note: Internal mahogany browning risk at 1-2 C; 3-4 C causes irreversible reducing-sugar buildup. Freezes at -1 C. Lowest respiration is at 2-3 C.
potato.respiration_source: chapter data, mature/cured vs immature tubers
potato.ethylene_note: Very low producer, low sensitivity. Cut/bruised tubers produce much more ethylene. Needs darkness (greening/solanine risk) — a physical shelf-design constraint, not a fan-control one.

leafy_greens.source_pages: AH-66 pp. 353-355 (data specific to spinach; handbook notes other cooking greens are expected in the same general range)
leafy_greens.variant_assumed: spinach used as reference proxy for leafy greens generally
leafy_greens.chilling_note: Not chilling sensitive — store as cold as possible without freezing. Freezing risk just below 0 C.
leafy_greens.shelf_life_note: ~2 weeks under proper cold handling; turnip greens far more perishable, kale up to 3 weeks. At kirana ambient temp (no active cooling) actual shelf life will be much shorter than these cold-chain figures.
leafy_greens.q10_note: Q10 is far from constant across this range and much higher than the other three commodities — leafy greens are the most temperature-sensitive commodity in this set by a wide margin.
leafy_greens.ethylene_note: Very low producer, but sensitive to external ethylene — accelerates yellowing/senescence. Co-storing with a moderate ethylene producer like tomato is a real design risk.

cross_commodity_notes: Respiration rate at 20 C, low to high: onion (8) < potato mature/cured (21.5) < tomato (34.5) << leafy greens (229.5). Leafy greens spoil roughly 7-10x faster than tomato at the same temperature and are the strongest single-commodity choice if the shelf needs to visibly demonstrate spoilage dynamics over a short demo window.
Onion and potato are comparatively shelf-stable (low, near-constant Q10) — a system tuned only for these two would show less dramatic before/after results.

Tomato is the only one of the four with meaningful ethylene production (1-10 uL/kg/h) AND meaningful ethylene sensitivity elsewhere (leafy greens) — do not co-locate tomato with leafy greens in the same monitored zone without accounting for this.

All four commodities' 'optimal storage' temperatures assume commercial cold-chain/wholesale conditions (0-21 C). A kirana shelf with only an exhaust fan (no active refrigeration) cannot reach these in most of India — the SRI/fan logic should be framed around minimizing deviation and venting heat/humidity/gas buildup relative to ambient, not hitting these absolute targets.
